skill.name: Sharpen vague words in a draft
skill.why: Blurry words make readers guess. Sharp words show exactly what you mean.
skill.how: Find the blurry word. Read the clues around it. Swap in the word that fits.

show.nudge: Woke is clear. We know exactly what happened.
Seven is exact. We know the time.

steps.ask: Tap the word that could mean almost anything.
steps.win: Yes! Thing could be anything. That's a blurry word.

steps.say: To sharpen it, I read the clues.

options.reason: Phones ring, but do they tick all night? Check every clue.
A rooster can wake you, but can it tick? Check every clue.

steps.win: Yes! A clock ticks and rings. It fits every clue.

steps.say: Bad is blurry too. Bad how? Zed's review has clues.
steps.ask: Which word says exactly what was wrong?

options.reason: Boring means dull. The clues are about the game breaking.
Scary means it frightens you. Check the clues: freezing and crashing.

steps.win: Yes! Glitchy fits freezing and crashing. Now it's exact.

steps.say: Blurry words can hide amounts too. Read Gus's notes.

show.nudge: Found is clear. We know what Gus did.
Three is exact. We know how many beetles.
Under is clear. We know where they were.

steps.win: Some worms: two? Fifty? Some and lots make readers guess.

steps.say: Verbs can be blurry too. Went doesn't show how something moved.

show.text: Its feet never touched the floor.

steps.ask: Which verb shows how the ghost moved?

options.reason: Stomping feet hit the floor hard. Check the clue about its feet.
Running feet touch the floor. Check the clue again.

steps.win: Yes! Feet that never touch the floor mean the ghost floated.

steps.say: Careful! Indi's draft says, 'The wave was big.'

show.text: The wave was very, very big.
show.nudge: Very, very makes it bigger, but can you see how big?

show.text: The wave was taller than the lighthouse.
The wave was the biggest wave ever.
show.nudge: Biggest compared to what? It's a boast. We still can't picture it.

steps.ask: Tap the edit that lets you picture the wave.
steps.win: You can picture it. Sharp means clear, not bigger or fancier.

terms.means: A word like thing, bad, some or went. It could mean almost anything.
Words nearby that tell you what the blurry word really means.
Fits every clue, so the reader can picture it exactly.

examples.text: The wave was taller than the lighthouse.

card.test: Find the blurry word. Read the clues. Pick the word that fits every clue, not the fanciest.

creature.name: Whetwing
creature.blurb: A peregrine falcon that sharpens its claws on the crater's black rock. Blurry words make it squint, but a sharp one sends it diving.

Glass is exact. It tells you what the drink was in.

Fizzy tells you about bubbles. The clues are about how cold it was.

encounters.frame: Zed's space report is full of sentences. The Whetwing only likes the sharp ones.
encounters.prompt: Is each sentence blurry or sharp? Sort them.
encounters.success: Blurry sentences use words like okay, lots and things. Sharp sentences show exactly what happened.

items.text: The launch went okay.
items.reason: Okay doesn't say what happened at the launch. The reader can't picture it.

items.text: The rocket roared off the launch pad.
items.reason: Roared tells you exactly how the rocket left.

items.text: The astronaut saw lots of things.
items.reason: Lots of things could be anything at all, so the reader has to guess.

items.text: A comet streaked past the window.
items.reason: Comet and streaked tell you exactly what went past and how.

items.text: The food in space was a bit weird.
items.reason: A bit weird doesn't say what the food was like. Was it dry? Runny?

Catchy means easy to remember. The clues are about how loud it was.

encounters.prompt: Which edit is sharper, and why?
encounters.success: Edit B. Eerie is a stronger word, but only B lets the reader see the sea.

options.text: Edit A, because eerie is a much stronger and more unusual word than strange.
options.reason: Stronger, but still blurry. Eerie gives a feeling, not what the sea looked like.

options.text: Edit B, because we can picture the flat water and the clouds in it.
Edit A, because it keeps the keeper's sentence and changes just one word.
options.reason: Changing one word is neat, but eerie is still blurry. It doesn't show what the sea looked like.

options.text: Edit B, because 'mirrored' is a fancier, more grown-up word than 'eerie'.
options.reason: Fancy words don't make it sharp. B wins because we can picture the flat sea.

encounters.frame: Indi tried seven edits of one blurry line in her gallery review. The Whetwing only wants the ones it can picture.
encounters.prompt: What did each edit do to Indi's line? Sort them.
encounters.success: More very, or a grander word, still leaves us guessing. Comparing with something we know lets us see it.

items.text: The gallery was really, really big.
items.reason: Really, really makes it bigger, but we still can't picture it.

items.text: The gallery was colossal.
items.reason: Colossal is a grander word for big. But how big? We still can't see it.

items.text: A footy oval could fit inside the gallery.
items.reason: We know how big an oval is, so we can picture the gallery.

items.text: The gallery was immense.

encounters.frame: Tully's report on the Reef Rays' final needs one sharper verb at the big moment.

body.reason: She caught it cleanly, which the draft calls a mark. Fumbling drops it. Punching hits it away.
